name: PT Ramayana Lestari Sentosa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Ramayana Lestari Sentosa: the cash is worth more than the stores the market is pricing
frontmatter.summary: We initiate on RALS at BUY with a Rp462 target and a 35.8% total return. The market capitalisation is barely above the liquid assets on the September 2026 balance sheet, so the stores are priced at little more than one year's EBITDA. Revenue is falling faster than the retail market, but the estate is profitable, the dividend is funded from cash, and the price discounts a permanent decline.
thesis: The equity trades at 0.6x book, and the Rp988.1bn of cash, Rp210.6bn of deposits and Rp892.3bn of short-term investments held at 30 September 2026 cover most of the market capitalisation even after deducting lease liabilities of Rp75.5bn and Rp311.3bn [S5].
Revenue fell -14.3% in FY2025 and falls -11.1% in FY2026E against a retail market growing 0.6% [S4][S7] - this is share loss, not a weak cycle.
Consignment commission of Rp495.6bn in nine months carries no cost of goods and lifted the group gross margin to 54.0% [S5].
The dividend is the return: 113% of FY2024 profit was paid out [S4], and our target assumes Rp43 over the next twelve months.
At Rp372 the reverse DCF needs FY2027E revenue growth of -17.1%, then a similar decline in every year to FY2035E; we forecast -3.0% in FY2027E and flat thereafter [S0].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Ramayana Lestari Sentosa Tbk with a **BUY** rating and a Rp462 target against a Rp372 price, a 35.8% total return including Rp43 of forecast dividend. Before scenarios the blended valuation is Rp485; weighted across our three scenarios it is Rp514, and the target we publish applies a liquidity discount to that [S0].

The call is not a bet on the retail cycle. The equity is valued at 0.6x book value, and the company held Rp988.1bn of cash, Rp210.6bn of term deposits and Rp892.3bn of short-term investments at 30 September 2026 against Rp75.5bn of current and Rp311.3bn of non-current lease liabilities [S5]. Net of the leases that leaves a liquid balance only slightly below the whole market capitalisation. What remains is an enterprise value for an estate of 91 Ramayana department stores and 57 Robinson supermarkets that is a little over one times the Rp528.5bn of EBITDA the business generated in FY2025 [S4]. Our DCF values the same operations at an enterprise value of Rp1,606.1bn, or Rp540 per share [S0]. Either the stores are terminal, or they are not.
Three things carry the value.

**First, the cash and the dividend.** At 30 September 2026 the company held Rp988.1bn of cash and equivalents, Rp210.6bn of term deposits and Rp892.3bn of short-term investments, against Rp75.5bn of current and Rp311.3bn of non-current lease liabilities [S5]. It has no bank debt and no bonds [S4], so virtually all of that liquid balance is surplus to the operating business. The company distributes effectively all of its earnings: Rp355.9bn was paid in 2025 out of FY2024 profits, a 113% payout [S4], and 50.0 per share was declared out of FY2025. Book value per share is 588.7 against a 0.6x price-to-book [S0]. The discount is not a distressed-balance-sheet discount - there is no debt to distress - it is a franchise discount.

**Second, a mix shift inside a shrinking top line.** Revenue fell -14.3% in FY2025 to Rp2,365.3bn [S4] and a further -11.1% in our FY2026 forecast, after nine months of Rp1,664.6bn [S5]. The fall is concentrated in the part of the business that carries inventory: outright sales were Rp1,169.0bn in the nine months while consignment commission - where a partner owns the stock and Ramayana takes a share of the sale - held at Rp495.6bn [S5]. Because commission revenue carries no cost of goods, the mix shift lifts the gross margin to 54.0% in our forecast from 52.4% in FY2025 [S4]. A smaller but higher-quality revenue base is a better starting point than the headline decline suggests.

**Third, the price already assumes decline.** Our reverse DCF asks what revenue path the current share price requires. The solver applies a single shock of -14.1% to the growth assumption in every forecast year, so the answer is not one bad year: at Rp372 the model needs FY2027E revenue growth of -17.1% and roughly the same decline in each of the following eight years, against our forecast of -3.0% in FY2027E and flat thereafter [S0]. That is a permanent, sustained contraction of the estate, not an accelerating collapse and not a one-off. The sensitivity work in the valuation section shows the target holds even if revenue growth is materially worse than we assume in every forecast year.

Two things would change our mind, and we state them up front. Revenue decline that continues after the outlet closures are complete would make the operating business genuinely terminal, and the cash would then be the only value in the name. And the related-party channel - Rp92.5bn of rent paid in FY2025 to PT Jakarta Intiland, 58.9% of the total lease bill, plus Rp35.1bn of repairs and maintenance charges to the same company and Rp42.8bn of revenue-sharing income from PT Milkyverse, 31.2% of other income [S4] - is how value could quietly leave a balance sheet this cash-rich. Both are treated in the risk and governance sections.

Ramayana is one of the oldest department-store operators in Indonesia. The format it built - a large multi-brand store aimed at lower- and middle-income shoppers - was the backbone of organised retail in the country for three decades before specialist apparel chains, minimarts and online marketplaces took share from it. Department-store retail is now a mature industry in which the size of a store network has stopped being a source of advantage, and in which the ability to convert floor space into rent and commission income is what separates survivors from casualties.

Ramayana operates a two-banner retail estate. At 31 December 2025 it operated 91 Ramayana department stores and 57 Robinson supermarket outlets, after closing outlets it judged unproductive as part of an ongoing estate review [S4]. The closures show up in the workforce: the company employed 5,257 people at the end of FY2025, a reduction of 404 on the prior year [S4].

The business earns revenue in two very different ways, and the difference is the key to the margin story. **Outright sales** are goods Ramayana buys and resells; they were Rp1,169.0bn in the first nine months of FY2026 and carry a cost of goods. **Consignment commission** is the company's share of a partner's sale proceeds where the partner owns the stock and Ramayana provides the space, the staff and the customer; it was Rp495.6bn in the same period at effectively no cost of goods [S5]. Commission revenue is close to pure margin and it is the part of the business that has held up, which is why the group gross margin has risen while revenue has fallen.

The company reports two segments. Fashion and accessories - the department stores and the great majority of consignment income - generated Rp1,866.8bn of revenue in FY2025 [S4]. Groceries, run through Robinson Supermarket, generated Rp494.0bn of outright sales [S4], roughly a fifth of group revenue. Groceries is the structurally weaker half: it produced Rp69.8bn of gross profit on that revenue, a gross margin in the mid-teens against well over half in fashion, and it ran a segment operating loss [S4]. The closure and conversion programme has been concentrated there, and the company describes it as a store transformation exercise rather than a growth plan [S4].

Alongside the retail operations the company earns Rp137.4bn of other income, which the income statement carries inside operating profit [S4]. The annual report attributes the increase to higher rental income from activities within the stores [S4]: Ramayana is increasingly a landlord to third-party tenants on its own floor space. That is a real, recurring, cash-generating activity, and it is the line the published data pack drops and our model restores (the financial analysis below).

The group is a single legal entity with no minority interests and no consolidated subsidiaries of consequence [S4][S5]. It has no bank borrowings and has never issued public debt; the whole debt line is lease liabilities, the present value of the rent obligations on the space it leases [S4]. Management's stated plan for FY2026 is to accelerate the performance recovery through marketing, product optimisation and operational efficiency, with a target of up to 5.0% growth in sales and net profit [S4]. The estate plan is defensive rather than expansionary: realised capex on owned fixed assets was Rp228.7bn in FY2025 and the company has held back new openings rather than expand [S4].

In this format the economics are driven by space productivity rather than store count. A department store earns a return on the floor area it controls: goods sold outright earn a mark-up once, while consigned goods earn a commission on a partner's capital and inventory risk. That is why the ratio of commission to outright revenue is watched so closely - it determines how much of a sales performance falls through to the company's own gross profit. The second lever is the rent paid for that space relative to the sales a store generates. Where both move against a retailer at once the operating leverage is severe, and closures take a long time to show up in the reported numbers.

Indonesian retail is growing, but slowly in real terms, and Ramayana is not keeping up with it. Bank Indonesia's real retail sales index grew 0.6% year on year in September 2026, and the central bank's own projection put the index at 222 index for October [S7][S8]. Against that, group revenue fell -14.3% in FY2025 [S4] and the first nine months of FY2026 came in at Rp1,664.6bn against Rp1,878.0bn a year earlier [S5]. Even in the strongest seasonal quarter of the year, the quarter that contains Ramadan and Lebaran, revenue was only Rp985.2bn [S2]. The gap between a flat-to-modestly-growing market and a double-digit revenue decline is the single most important fact about this company.

The driver deck this name depends on is the house macro deck, and its message is unfriendly. It projects the rupiah at 18,350 to the dollar, Indonesian CPI at 3.3% and real GDP growth at 5.3% [S0]. Household consumption is therefore still growing, and a retailer with the right format can grow in this environment. The problem for Ramayana is the format, not the macro.

The competitive pressure comes from two directions at once. At the value end, low-price general merchandise formats - the phenomenon the Indonesian press has dubbed "Rojali" and "Rohana" - have taken the price-led shopper who was Ramayana's historical customer. At the other end, single-brand and specialist apparel chains take the aspirational shopper. Online marketplaces take a slice of both, particularly in the categories where a department store has the most floor space to fill. Price competition in the categories the company sells is intense and deflationary in real terms [S7].

Where does that leave the moat? Thin, and narrowing. The distribution argument for Indonesian retail - reach across islands, density of store networks, logistics into secondary cities - is the standard quality moat in this market, and Ramayana has a genuine island-wide footprint built over four decades [S4]. What it does not have is pricing power, brand scarcity or switching costs: a shopper can substitute the store, the format or the channel at essentially no cost. Buyer power is high and rising because alternative channels are plentiful. Supplier power is low but moving in the suppliers' favour, which is exactly what the steady shift from outright goods to consignment records: the brand owner sets the terms and keeps the inventory risk. Substitutes are plentiful and multiplying. New entrants are constrained by the difficulty of assembling good retail sites, but that protection applies equally to the incumbents and has not saved the format. Rivalry is intense.

The structural response visible in the filings is a retreat to a smaller, better-screened estate, a higher-margin mix, and monetisation of floor space through rent [S4]. That is a rational strategy for a company with a large cash pile and a shrinking franchise. It also means the right valuation question is not when growth resumes, but what the remaining cash-generating capacity of the estate is worth and what the cash is worth - which is how the valuation is built.

Indonesian organised retail went through a long expansion as consumers moved from traditional markets to modern formats, then a shakeout as online commerce and smaller-format convenience retail absorbed much of that growth. Department stores, which need large sites and depend on discretionary fashion sales, were the format most exposed. When a store's sales fall its cost base does not immediately follow, because rent and staffing are largely fixed, so a modest revenue decline produces a large profit decline and a visible store-closure cycle. Sector surveys have repeatedly noted footfall pressure in shopping centres, and the standard industry response has been a mix shift towards consignment and rent income rather than new space.

**History.** FY2025 revenue was Rp2,365.3bn, down -14.3%, with gross profit of Rp1,239.1bn and a gross margin of 52.4% [S4]. Operating profit - the LK's *Laba Usaha* - was Rp195.6bn, net profit Rp265.3bn and earnings per share 44.7 [S4]. The nine months to September 2026 show the same shape at a lower level: revenue of Rp1,664.6bn and operating profit of Rp210.4bn, with net profit of Rp237.5bn [S5]. Net profit held up better than operating profit for a different reason than the cash pile: the income tax charge fell from Rp42.3bn to Rp23.2bn, while finance income fell to Rp118.8bn from Rp131.9bn as short-term investments were drawn down [S4]. The cash pile is still a large fraction of the year's net profit, but it did not grow it in FY2025.

**A restatement you need to know about.** The published data pack's FY2025 operating profit is roughly two-fifths of the audited figure, because the pack strips out Rp137.4bn of other income and Rp13.5bn of other expenses that the Indonesian statement of profit or loss carries inside operating profit [S4]. The audited bridge is simple: gross profit of Rp1,239.1bn, less total operating expenses of Rp1,167.4bn, plus other income of Rp137.4bn, less other expenses of Rp13.5bn, equals operating profit of Rp195.6bn [S4]. Most of that other income is rent charged to tenants in the stores [S4]. We restate to the audited line, and the reason is not cosmetic: if the rental income is treated as non-operating it also leaves the cash flow we discount, which understates enterprise value by more than a hundred billion rupiah a year.

The same correction has to be made to the expense line, and this is where a gross and a net definition can part company. Our opex line is the one that sits between gross profit and operating profit in the model, so it is total selling and administrative expenses less other income plus other expenses: Rp1,043.5bn in FY2025 and Rp1,137.5bn in FY2024, not the Rp1,167.4bn and Rp1,220.5bn the LK prints before other income [S4]. On that definition gross profit less opex equals the audited Laba Usaha in each of the three years the FY2025 annual report shows: FY2025 is Rp1,239.1bn less Rp1,043.5bn, equal to the audited Rp195.6bn, and FY2023 is Rp1,391.8bn less Rp1,144.8bn, equal to the audited Rp247.0bn [S4]. FY2022A is the one historical year we cannot tie out, because the annual report carries only three comparative columns; that year stays on the data pack's own operating-profit definition and is shown in the table for reference only. The forecast uses the same definition, so the expense ratios in the next paragraph are comparable with the history.

**The revenue build.** We forecast FY2026E revenue of Rp2,102.8bn, a fall of -11.1% - the nine months already delivered plus a fourth quarter in line with the prior year's weak fourth quarter [S4][S5]. For FY2027E we assume -3.0%, the year in which the outlet-closure programme laps, and then hold revenue flat in nominal rupiah through FY2035E on the assumption of no new openings [S4][S6]. This is deliberately below management's stated target for FY2026 [S4], because the nine months have already missed that target by a wide margin. Anchoring on management's plan would require ignoring the actual numbers; anchoring on the nine-month run-rate is what the evidence supports.

**Margins.** We hold the gross margin at 54.0%, above what FY2025 delivered but below the nine-month rate, because the consignment mix keeps rising while the fourth quarter is the discount-heavy quarter [S4][S5]. Operating expenses on the definition above were Rp1,043.5bn in FY2025 against revenue of Rp2,365.3bn, and we forecast 45.5% of revenue for FY2026E - a higher ratio than FY2025, because the fourth quarter carries the full cost base into the discount-heavy sales month, as it did in FY2025 [S4]. From FY2027E the ratio drifts down to 44.3% by FY2030E: other income rose from Rp109.4bn in FY2024 to Rp137.4bn in FY2025 and was Rp118.6bn in the first nine months of FY2026 against Rp96.2bn a year earlier, it is contractual rent from tenants inside the stores, and SG&A falls as outlets close, so a flat ratio would assume the fastest-growing line in the P&L stops growing [S4][S5]. The result is a forecast operating margin of 8.5% and operating profit of Rp178.7bn in FY2026E, consistent with the nine months delivered plus a seasonally weak fourth quarter [S5]. Negative operating leverage is real in FY2026E and then eases; it is not permanent in the model.

**Depreciation, capex and the lease question.** Total depreciation and amortisation was Rp332.9bn in FY2025, and most of it is depreciation of leased store space rather than owned buildings [S4]. It is a rent charge in substance. The nine-month figure is Rp278.6bn on revenue of Rp1,664.6bn [S5], and we carry 17.0% of revenue for FY2026E before fading to 15.0% as the depreciable base shrinks. Because we carry the lease liabilities in debt we must also treat right-of-use additions as capex: total capex in FY2025 was Rp458.4bn, of which Rp228.7bn was owned fixed assets and the balance additions to right-of-use assets during a lease-renewal wave [S4]. We forecast capex at 15.0% of revenue, above the three-year average and equal to the terminal depreciation rate, so the terminal year reinvests one for one and no value comes from permanent under-investment. Because net reinvestment in the terminal year is nil, terminal growth is set to zero in the valuation section: there is no capital behind growth, and we do not pay for any.

**Balance sheet and cash.** The company has no bank debt and no bonds. The debt we carry into our forecasts is lease liabilities, split at 30 September 2026 between Rp75.5bn current and Rp311.3bn non-current [S5]. Against that sat Rp988.1bn of cash and equivalents, Rp210.6bn of term deposits and Rp892.3bn of short-term investments, and those balances are genuinely liquid - the company monetised short-term investments through the investing line during FY2025 [S4]. Equity was Rp3,492.0bn at the last year-end, or 588.7 per share [S4].

**Cash conversion and earnings quality.** Cash generated from operations was Rp577.7bn in FY2025 against net profit of Rp265.3bn [S4], so cash earnings comfortably exceed accounting earnings - the opposite of the accruals warning sign. Working capital is negative, Rp-115.2bn or about minus five percent of revenue [S0], because suppliers and consignment partners fund the inventory and customer prepayments sit on the balance sheet as a source of funds. Receivables are immaterial at a few billion rupiah [S5], which rules out the receivable-stuffing flag, and inventory days have not deteriorated as revenue has fallen [S5]. The two quality issues we would flag are that the effective tax rate is well below statutory - part of the finance income is taxed at source - and that a persistent share of net profit is finance income rather than trading profit, which is why the P/E cross-check in the valuation section is a weak test for this name.

**Capital allocation.** The company pays out essentially everything it earns: Rp355.9bn of cash dividend for FY2024, a 113% payout, after 98.7% for FY2023 [S4], and 50.0 per share for FY2025, 111.8% of that year's net profit [S4][S5]. That payout is total dividend over total profit, so it does not change with the share count; what the treasury reissuance changes is the per-share rate, which now spreads over 6,134.8m shares rather than the 5,931.3m outstanding when the dividend was declared [S4][S5]. It reissued treasury shares during the first nine months of FY2026, cutting the treasury block to 961 million shares [S5], which raised cash and reduced the overhang. With no debt and no expansion plan we carry the company's own 113.0% record rather than a notional lower payout. On that level the dividend exceeds accounting earnings but is still funded from free cash flow plus after-tax finance income - the FY2026E FCFF of Rp189.0bn plus finance income of Rp105.4bn comes close to covering the Rp296.6bn we model as paid - and the cash pile is the buffer in any year where the two do not meet [S0]. The risk is therefore not immediate funding but the pace at which the pile is drawn down.

Indonesian issuers report cash flow under the direct method and account for leases under the local equivalent of the international lease standard. Long-term rent obligations are capitalised as a right-of-use asset with a matching lease liability, and the old rent expense is split into depreciation and interest. For a retailer with a large leased estate this changes both the reported EBITDA margin and the reported debt, and it means two retailers with identical cash rents can show very different EBITDA. The convention that keeps comparisons honest is the one used here: put the lease liability in net debt and the right-of-use additions in capex, so rent is treated as an investment rather than as a free lunch.

We use the house method set for discretionary retail: a discounted cash flow to the firm as the primary method at a 60% weight, a price-to-earnings cross-check at 30% and an EV/EBITDA cross-check at 10% [S0]. The weights are the industry default and they fit this name specifically: the DCF is the only method that can price a business whose operating cash flow and whose cash pile are of similar size, while the earnings and EBITDA multiples are applied to a profit and loss account that is heavily supported by finance income.

**Cost of capital.** The build is in the table above and here it is line by line, because the arithmetic matters to the conclusion. The rupiah risk-free rate is 7.4%, less a sovereign default spread of 1.6% because the risk-free rate is struck in a currency that can default and the equity premium is not; the beta is the industry default unlevered 0.90, re-levered to 1.02 at the company's minimal debt-to-equity of 0.17; and the equity risk premium is the mature-market 4.2% plus the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5% [S0]. Cost of equity is therefore 7.4% minus 1.6% plus 1.02 times the sum of 4.2% and 2.5%, which is 12.6%. On the debt side we use the house corporate cost of debt of 9.4% rather than the implicit lease rate the company actually pays [S4] - the conservative side - at a 14.5% weight and the statutory 22.0% tax shield, giving a weighted average cost of capital of 11.9%. We apply no premium or discount on top. The default-spread adjustment is the reason the cost of equity reads 12.6% rather than the 7.4% plus beta-times-premium figure the same inputs would give without it, and it is the house convention for every rupiah valuation rather than a name-specific choice.
**The DCF.**

The model runs a ten-year explicit horizon to FY2035E and capitalises the final year's free cash flow at the weighted average cost of capital with no growth: terminal growth is 0.0% [S0]. That is not a cautious assumption bolted on; it is the arithmetic of the business we model. In the terminal year capex equals depreciation at 15.0% of revenue and operating working capital is negative and roughly stable, so the reinvestment rate is nil. Return on incremental invested capital is therefore also nil on the marginal rupiah - there is no new capital to earn a return on. With no reinvestment there is no growth to pay for: g equals reinvestment rate times return on incremental capital, which is zero, and with the return on the existing capital base we source no widening moat, the excess return fades to the cost of capital rather than persisting forever [S4][S7]. Free cash flow to the firm is Rp189.0bn in FY2026E and the terminal value is 34.1% of enterprise value. The DCF produces an enterprise value of Rp1,606.1bn for the operating business and, after adding net cash and deducting lease liabilities, Rp540 per share.

The terminal value deserves a second test, because a DCF with a zero-growth terminal can still smuggle in a large exit multiple. Ours does, and we state it plainly. The discounted terminal value is 34.1% of the Rp1,606.1bn DCF enterprise value, and it exceeds the entire enterprise value the market currently puts on the same estate only when that market value is struck on the model's own FY2026E net debt line of Rp-1,822.8bn - negative, so a net cash balance carried forward on our cash-flow forecast. On the 30 September 2026 reported net cash, which is the smaller figure and the one the DCF's own bridge deducts, the market's enterprise value is higher and the discounted terminal value comes out about the size of it rather than above it. Struck on FY2035E EBITDA of Rp509.9bn, the terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA of about three times and an exit EV/EBIT of about seven and a half times, against an entry of about one times EBITDA - 0.8x on the model's cash roll-forward and a little over one times on the reported balance sheet - and about three times operating profit. The multiple-survival test therefore fails on its face: the DCF capitalises the terminal year at getting on for three times the multiple the market pays today, and we say so rather than dress the terminal value up as a fade. What the DCF does not assume is that the re-rating keeps going after the first forecast year, because the exit multiple is struck on an FY2035E operating profit of Rp204.0bn that is only modestly above the FY2025 audited figure [S4][S0]. The honest reading is that the DCF does not need the business to recover, only for terminal operating profit to hold, and that everything in the call rests on durability rather than growth - which is exactly what the risk section stress-tests.
**Cross-checks, and why they disagree.**

The P/E leg gives Rp363, -32.7% against the DCF, at a multiple of 8.4 times. The EV/EBITDA leg gives Rp527, -2.4% against the DCF, at 2.9 times. The divergence between the DCF and the P/E leg is the whole investment case and it deserves an honest explanation rather than a smoothing exercise.

The P/E multiple is a blend of the peer median and the company's own history, and the company's own history is a de-rated history: the market has spent years marking this franchise down, and the 8.3x trailing multiple in the table is struck on the 5,931.3m shares outstanding at the last year-end, before the treasury reissuance; on the 6,134.8m shares now outstanding the same trailing profit is a lower per-share figure and the market pays a little over eight and a half times at the Rp372 price. Either way it is a single-digit trailing multiple, which is the market's verdict on the operating business. Applying that multiple to earnings that are heavily supported by finance income of Rp118.8bn [S4] essentially re-derives today's share price, so the leg is a circular test of the market's own conclusion; that is why we weight it below the DCF. The EV/EBITDA leg, which nets the cash out of the enterprise value and so is not contaminated in the same way, lands within a few percent of the DCF. One caveat on that leg: its own-history sample runs over four years and only FY2023A-FY2025A could be restated to the audited operating-profit definition [S4]; the FY2022A point uses the data pack's definition, which understates profit and so biases that one multiple, and therefore the leg, marginally upward rather than down.

**How the market multiple is measured.** One convention needs stating because it drives the headline "cheap" impression. The display multiples in this report use each forecast year's modelled net debt, not today's reported balance sheet. The model carries the liquid balance forward on its own cash-flow forecast, and for FY2026E that produces a larger net cash position after lease liabilities than the 30 September 2026 accounts show; a larger net cash balance lowers enterprise value, so the display EV/EBITDA is 0.9x. On the balance sheet actually reported at 30 September 2026 - cash Rp988.1bn, term deposits Rp210.6bn and short-term investments Rp892.3bn against lease liabilities of Rp75.5bn current and Rp311.3bn non-current [S5] - the same market capitalisation implies an enterprise value a little over one times FY2025 EBITDA, not the sub-one-times figure the display multiple shows. Both are correct under their own convention; the reported-balance-sheet figure is the one to quote when comparing with a peer, and it is still cheap.

**What we do not add to the bridge.** The post-balance-sheet review found no announced capital action to value: no buyback, no treasury cancellation, no special dividend, no asset sale and no material acquisition between the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet date and today [S4][S5]. The one capital action in the period was the sale of treasury shares, which raised cash and is already reflected in the share count. We therefore add nothing to the bridge rather than inventing an option value. The cash is counted at face value in net debt, so a buyback at the current discount to book would transfer value between holders without changing our number, and a special dividend would be value-neutral by construction. A capital-return announcement is an upside risk to the timing of the re-rating, not to the value itself.

**What the price implies.** At Rp372 the reverse DCF holds the method set fixed and solves for the revenue growth that reproduces today's value. The solver applies one additive shock of -14.1% to our revenue growth in every forecast year, so the answer is a path, not a point: FY2027E growth of -17.1% against our -3.0%, then a decline of similar size in each of the following eight years, compounding to roughly a fifth of today's revenue by the end of the explicit horizon [S0]. That is the cleanest statement of our variant view. The market is not pricing one bad year and it is not pricing an accelerating collapse; it is pricing a sustained, decade-long contraction at a fairly even rate, and that is a different and more demanding claim about the business than a trough year followed by stabilisation.
**Sensitivity.**

The first grid flexes the discount rate and terminal growth around the DCF; the second flexes revenue growth and gross margin around the target. The second grid is the one that matters for this name: the target survives materially worse revenue growth than we assume in every forecast year, because the net cash position and the low enterprise value do the work. Below that, the cash floor takes over.

Finally we apply a 10.0% liquidity discount, because three-month average daily turnover is far too thin for a position of any size to be built or exited without moving the price [S0]. That takes the probability-weighted value of Rp514 to the Rp462 we publish. The method set suits this industry because retail value ultimately rests on the cash a store estate can generate and on the property and cash behind it, and the DCF is the only leg here that can price both.
**Scenario analysis.**

The base case carries twice the weight of each wing, and the wings are mirrored on purpose. Revenue growth, gross margin and capex are each shocked by the same amount in opposite directions; the bear additionally carries one one-sided shock, a two-point rise in the operating-expense ratio when the related-party rental income from PT Milkyverse is not renewed. That shock is not mirrored because no filing gives a sourced upside in the same contract - renewal on current terms is already in the base case - and the asymmetry is recorded in the model notes rather than hidden [S4].

The bear also carries the cash-side shock the method asks for: capex one point of revenue higher, which is what further closures, re-fitting and severance cost a retailer that has to exit space it had planned to keep. The bear case is worth Rp404, the bull Rp643, against Rp504 in the base case. Note what that means: even the bear does not take the share below the Rp372 at which it trades today.

The probability-weighted value sits above the base value, and we should explain the arithmetic because it looks like conviction we do not have. Roughly three quarters of the market capitalisation is net cash. A given proportional hit to the operating enterprise value therefore moves the share price by less than that proportion, and the one-sided bear shock is partly offset by the cash the business retains when earnings fall, because the payout is a percentage of a lower profit. The capex shock cuts the other way: a one-point capex saving is worth more rupiah in the bull, where revenue is higher, than the one-point increase costs in the bear. The convexity is real but it is arithmetic, not a stronger case, and the published target applies the liquidity discount on top of it.
**Downside risks, ranked by likelihood times impact.**

*Revenue decline does not stop (high likelihood, high impact).* This is the central risk. The nine months of FY2026 delivered revenue of Rp1,664.6bn against a market growing 0.6% in real terms [S5][S7]. If the closures address a symptom - too much space - rather than the cause, shoppers leaving the format, then a smaller estate is simply a smaller declining business and the operating profit of Rp178.7bn we forecast has no moat around it. The evidence cuts both ways: closing unproductive stores should lift the average, but nine months of reporting show the remaining estate still shrinking [S5].

*Consumer weakness in a rate-sensitive sector (medium likelihood, medium impact).* The house macro regime is cautious on balance-of-payments pressure and averse to Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer discretionary, so this name sits on the wrong side of the house tilt. We are not leaning against the tilt for its own sake: the deck we are required to use projects CPI at 3.3% and real GDP growth of 5.3%, an environment of stable, unspectacular consumption rather than contraction [S0]. The company's own customer base, lower and middle income, is the most rate-sensitive part of it.

*Related-party leakage (medium likelihood, high impact).* Three flows matter, and we quantify all of them. Lease payments of Rp92.5bn in FY2025 - 58.9% of every rupiah of rent the company paid - went to PT Jakarta Intiland, a related party of the controlling shareholder, and repairs and maintenance of a further Rp35.1bn, 3.2% of total general and administrative expenses, went to the same company [S4]. In the other direction, revenue-sharing income of Rp42.8bn, 31.2% of other income, came from PT Milkyverse Indonesia, against a fraction of that a year earlier [S4]. The income side is the more fragile of the two: it is a related-party agreement with no disclosed term, and it now supplies a third of the operating-income line our valuation depends on, which is why its non-renewal is the one unmirrored bear shock. We have no evidence the rent or the service charges are above market and cannot verify a market rate from public filings; but a cash-rich company paying the majority of its rent to a family vehicle, and booking growing income from another, is the standard channel through which value leaves minority shareholders in this market. It should be monitored rather than assumed benign.

*Dividend coverage (medium likelihood, medium impact).* The payout has exceeded accounting earnings in two of the last three years, at 113.0% of profit [S4]. It is funded from free cash flow plus finance income, not from accounting profit, and the cash pile is the buffer when the two do not meet. In a cash-flow valuation a cut is not directly value-destructive - the cash stays in the business and our FCFF does not change - so we do not model one. What it would destroy is the re-rating that depends on the dividend record, so it stays on the signpost list as a downgrade trigger rather than as a driver of the bear case.

*Liquidity and index treatment (high likelihood, low to medium impact).* Turnover is thin, which we have already priced through the liquidity discount [S0]. On the register, the controller PT Ramayana Makmursentosa holds 55.9%, the company holds 16.4% in treasury, the two disclosed directors hold 3.7% and 0.8%, and the shares held by the public, each below five percent, are 23.2% of the issued total; all holders below five percent together are 27.7% [S4]. The data pack's free float of 20.1% is its own estimate on a different basis, and we quote the register. Separately, the exchange has widened its high-shareholding-concentration screen to all listed companies without a market-cap floor, and names on that list have been excluded from the index calculation, with the revised rule effective alongside the list published on 11 November 2026 [S9]. RALS is not named in the sources available to us, so we assume no index event - but a thinner index presence would shrink the buyer base further.

*Governance and structure (low likelihood, medium impact).* The 16.4% treasury block is a latent source of dilution: reissuing treasury shares below book value transfers value away from existing holders, and it has already happened once this year [S5]. We find no evidence of manipulation-class behaviour - cash conversion is strong, receivables are immaterial and the audit opinion is clean [S4] - so we treat this as an optics-class flag.

**Signposts that would change our view.** We would upgrade if two consecutive quarters showed revenue growth no worse than the market's, if the company announced a defined end to the closure programme with a stable estate, or if management committed to returning excess cash through a special dividend or a buyback at a discount to book. We would move to HOLD or SELL if revenue decline accelerates for another year, if the dividend is cut, if a material related-party transaction is announced on terms we cannot assess, or if the cash pile falls materially without a matching reduction in the loss-making groceries footprint.

**Ownership and control.** PT Ramayana Makmursentosa, the controlling shareholder, holds 55.9% of the issued shares and the company holds 16.4% in treasury [S4]. The two disclosed directors hold 3.7% and 0.8%, and public shareholders each below five percent hold 23.2%; all holders below five percent, directors included, hold 27.7% [S4]. We state the basis because the data pack's free float of 20.1% is its own estimate: on the register, the shares not held by the controller or in treasury are 27.7% gross and the truly public holding is 23.2% [S4][S0]. Control is concentrated and unassailable in practice. That matters for how minority interests are treated - not because anything improper is visible, but because the register gives minorities no leverage. The exchange has revised its high-shareholding-concentration rule and published a new list on 11 November 2026, with names on it excluded from the index calculation [S9]; RALS does not appear in the sources available to us, and we treat index exclusion as a liquidity risk rather than a base-case event.

**Board and audit.** The FY2025 financial statements were audited by KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, with a clean opinion, and were published in March 2026 [S4]. The firm is mid-tier rather than a Big Four affiliate. We found no auditor change, no qualification and no disclosed administrative sanction or material legal case in the period under review [S4].

**Related-party dealings.** Two flows are large enough to quantify against the P&L. On the cost side, lease payments of Rp92.5bn went to PT Jakarta Intiland in FY2025 - 58.9% of total lease payments - and repairs and maintenance of Rp35.1bn went to the same company, 3.2% of total general and administrative expenses [S4]. On the income side, revenue-sharing income of Rp42.8bn came from PT Milkyverse Indonesia, 31.2% of other income, against a fraction of that a year earlier [S4]. The same note separately discloses related-party rental income from store space of Rp26.4bn, down on the prior year, and a revenue-sharing total of Rp43.0bn of which Milkyverse is all but a fraction [S4]. No term or renewal date is given for either agreement [S4]. Smaller balances - a trade payable to a related apparel supplier, security deposits to the same property company, and a joint arrangement with a related children's playground operator inside the stores - are all with entities associated with the controlling family [S4]. The income side is the item to watch: it is growing, it is a third of the operating-income line, and it is the only flow we model as vulnerable in the bear case.

**Capital allocation and dividends.** The dividend record is generous and consistent: a 113% payout for FY2024, after 98.7% for FY2023, and 50.0 per share declared for FY2025, 111.8% of that year's earnings - a ratio of totals that is invariant to the share count, though the per-share rate now spreads over the 6,134.8m shares outstanding after the treasury reissuance [S4][S5]. A company with no debt and a shrinking business that returns all of its profit is doing the right thing with the cash, and that is a meaningful part of why we are buyers - though the payout is funded from cash and finance income rather than from trading profit, which is why we treat a cut as a re-rating risk rather than as a funding event.

**Structure flags.** We checked the standard list: no pledge of the controlling stake is disclosed, no serial rights issue, no change of auditor, no receivables financing and no off-balance-sheet vehicle [S4]. The one item in the watch column is the treasury stock overhang of 16.4% of issued shares, part-reissued during the current year [S5].

**ESG.** The sustainability disclosures cover the usual ground for an Indonesian retailer of this size. The exposure that matters commercially is workforce: the company removed 404 roles during FY2025 [S4], and further reductions are a plausible part of any further cost programme, which carries industrial-relations and reputational risk. On governance, the concentrated ownership and the related-party rent line are the two disclosures most likely to move the share price. On the social side the customer base is low- and middle-income households, so the affordability of the offer is a reputational asset as well as a commercial one. The audit opinion is clean, no sanctions are disclosed, and there is no manipulation-class flag.

**Dated catalysts.** - **FY2026 results, February 2027:** the first hard test of whether the closures have stopped and revenue has stabilised, and the point at which our FY2026E revenue forecast of Rp2,102.8bn can be checked against the outturn [S4]. - **FY2026 dividend declaration, May 2027:** management's capital-allocation statement for the year; our target assumes Rp43 per share over the next twelve months [S4]. - **The monthly Bank Indonesia real retail sales index:** the cleanest read on whether Ramayana's decline is company-specific or market-wide; it grew 0.6% in September 2026 [S7]. - **Any statement on treasury reissuance or a capital-return programme:** the 16.4% treasury block is the largest structural item on the register [S4].

**Key performance indicators we watch between updates.** Revenue split between outright sales and consignment commission, because the mix drives the margin; the number of Ramayana and Robinson outlets per reporting period, which tells us whether the closure programme is finished; the gross margin, which should keep rising while the consignment shift continues; the other-income line, which is the rental monetisation of the floor space; cash, deposits and short-term investments, which are the floor under the valuation; lease payments to PT Jakarta Intiland as a share of the total, which is the governance barometer; and the effective tax rate, which has run well below statutory [S4][S5].

**What would make us wrong.** The most likely way this call fails is not an accounting problem or a governance scandal but a simple one: the stores keep losing customers faster than the cost base can shrink, as the nine-month revenue of Rp1,664.6bn against Rp1,878.0bn a year earlier records [S5], the operating profit we forecast becomes zero, and the shares become a cash shell trading at a discount that never closes. We accept that possibility - it is what the bear case is for - and we judge it less likely than the price implies.

bear.narrative: Share loss accelerates as budget formats and online take the middle-income shopper; closures run ahead of plan, gross margin falls on clearance, the related-party rental agreement behind Rp42.8bn of other income is not renewed, and further closures carry severance and fit-out cash costs.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the nine months delivered (-11.4% yoy [S5]) plus a fourth quarter in line with the FY2025 Q4 run-rate. FY2027E -3.0% assumes the unproductive-outlet closure programme [S4] laps through the year while the remaining estate stabilises. From FY2028E revenue is held flat in nominal rupiah, at exactly 0.0% for FY2028E, FY2029E and FY2030E and for the long-term rate: there is no sourced plan for new openings and management is holding back expansion capex [S6], so any like-for-like inflation in the remaining stores is offset by store-count attrition and continued share loss to specialist chains and online. The market proxy grew only 0.6% yoy [S7] against a group decline of 14.3%, so the historical gap is Ramayana-specific, not market-wide; we do not extrapolate the double-digit decline into perpetuity, but we also do not credit nominal GDP growth to an estate that is not opening stores.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin was 55.8% against 52.4% for FY2025 [S5][S4] because the consignment-commission mix rose to 29.8% of revenue from 27.1%: commission revenue carries no cost of goods, while the outright business earns a stable 37.1% margin [S5]. We hold 54.0% for the full year rather than the nine-month rate because the fourth quarter is the discount-heavy quarter and delivered only 47.5% in FY2025 [S4].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Opex here is selling plus general and administrative expenses less other income plus other expenses - the definition that makes gross profit less opex equal the LK's audited operating profit ('Laba Usaha'), which is struck after Rp137.4bn of other income that is mostly rent charged to tenants [S4]. Restated on that definition FY2025 was 44.1% of revenue (F52) and 9M2026 was 43.2% [S5]. FY2026E rises to 45.5% because the fourth quarter carries the full cost base on the discount-heavy sales month, matching the 54%-type fourth-quarter ratio in FY2025. Thereafter we let the ratio drift down 0.3pp a year, not hold it flat: other income grew 25.6% in FY2025 and 23.3% in 9M2026 while revenue fell [S4][S5], it is contractual rent from tenants inside the stores, and SG&A falls as outlets close, so a flat ratio would assume the fastest-growing line stops growing.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: D&A of Rp332.9bn in FY2025 [S4] is mostly depreciation of leased store space, so it is a rent charge in substance: right-of-use assets were Rp824.0bn at end-2025 [S4]. The nine-month figure is Rp278.6bn, 16.7% of nine-month revenue [S5]. We start at 17.0% of revenue for FY2026E - above the nine-month rate because the fourth quarter carries a full quarter of depreciation on a lower sales base - and fade to 15.0% because capex is below D&A, so the depreciable base shrinks.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total capex must include right-of-use additions because the lease liabilities they create sit in net debt: FY2025 was Rp228.7bn of owned fixed assets plus Rp229.7bn of right-of-use additions [S4], 19.4% of revenue, but that was a renewal spike. The three-year average is Rp284bn, or 12.0% of FY2025 revenue, and we carry 15.0% - above the three-year average and equal to the terminal D&A rate, so the terminal year reinvests one-for-one and no value comes from permanent under-investment.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital: suppliers and consignment partners fund the inventory, and contract liabilities are customer prepayments. FY2025 was -4.9% of revenue and FY2024 -5.2% [S0].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Effective rate has run at 8.1% in FY2025, 11.9% in FY2024 and 11.1% in 9M2026 [S4][S5]; part of the finance income is taxed at source. We use 11.0%, the middle of the observed range, rather than the 22% statutory rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The company has no interest-bearing bank debt; the balance-sheet debt is entirely lease liabilities. The implicit rate on those is 5.2% (Rp25.8bn interest on Rp500.6bn opening lease liabilities) [S4].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: The model applies the yield to opening cash, so the comparison must use the opening balance. FY2025 finance income of Rp118.8bn on Rp2,670.2bn of opening liquid assets is a 4.45% yield; the nine months of FY2026 annualise to Rp105.9bn on opening liquid assets of Rp2,291.8bn (cash Rp1,465.4bn, deposits Rp50.0bn, short-term investments Rp776.4bn, F61-F63), a 4.6% yield [S4][S5]. We use 4.6%; the 5.18% obtained by dividing FY2025 income by the closing balance is not the basis on which the model applies the rate.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No bank borrowing is planned and the company is not a lease-expansion story; lease liabilities are assumed to roll at existing levels.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Nil: the LK shows nothing between operating profit plus net finance income and pre-tax profit [S4].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interests on the balance sheet [S4].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company distributes more than it earns: 113.3% of FY2024 profit and 98.7% of FY2023 [S4]. The FY2025 dividend of Rp50 per share is 111.8% of FY2025 net profit on the 5,931.3m shares outstanding when it was declared (Rp296.6bn over Rp265.3bn) and 115.6% on the current 6,134.8m shares (Rp306.7bn over Rp265.3bn); the model's payout ratio uses the declared share count. We carry 113% of earnings - the audited FY2024 ratio, between the two FY2025 readings - because the cash pile funds the shortfall and there is no sourced plan to deploy the excess.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The data pack's last fiscal-year share count is the 31 December 2025 outstanding 5,931.3m; the company sold 203.5m treasury shares during 2026 and the outstanding count is now 6,134.8m [S5]. We step the count up once in FY2026E to 6,134.8m so EPS, DPS and BVPS agree with the 6,134.8m the valuation legs and the market capitalisation use, then hold it flat - no further reissuance is assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Zero, because the terminal year reinvests nothing net: capex equals D&A at 15% of revenue and working capital is negative, so the reinvestment rate is about nil and any positive g would be growth with no capital behind it. Section 2 finds a thin and narrowing moat and we can source no widening one, so g = reinvestment rate x ROIIC = 0, and the FY2035E FCFF is capitalised at WACC - the method card's fade to cost of capital with no excess-return growth [S4][S7].

challenges.challenge: The cost-of-capital paragraph cannot be reconciled with the model it prices. From the stated build - rf 7.4%, mature ERP 4.2%, country premium 2.5%, beta 0.90 re-levered to 1.02 - the cost of equity is 7.4 plus 1.02 times 6.7 = 14.2%, not the 12.6% printed, and the WACC comes to about 13.2%, outside the house 11-13% band. The engine reaches 12.65% only by subtracting a 1.62% default spread (fund record valuation.coc: rf 0.0745 - 0.0162 + 1.01897 x 0.0669) that the report never mentions. The sensitivity grid prices the WACC at about Rp24 a share per 1pp, so the undisclosed adjustment is worth roughly Rp40 on the DCF leg.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now prints the full build: risk-free 7.4% less the 1.62% sovereign default spread, plus beta 1.02 times the sum of the 4.2% mature premium and 2.5% country premium, giving a 12.6% cost of equity and 11.9% WACC inside the house band [S0]. The adjustment is the house rupiah convention and is now disclosed rather than implicit.

challenges.challenge: The opex driver changes definition between history and forecast. Model FY2025A opex is Rp1,167.4bn, 49.4% of revenue, and gross profit 1,239.06 less that opex is Rp71.6bn, not the Rp195.58bn the same model carries on the ebit line; FY2024A gives Rp172.4bn against an EBIT of Rp255.46bn. The forecast is 45.5% net of other income, so the assumptions compare 44.1% with 45.5% while the model runs 49.4% to 45.5%, and section 3 tells the reader the forecast implies a higher expense ratio than FY2025 when the model shows a 3.9pp improvement. The 2.4x restatement the analyst flagged is therefore visible on the EBIT line but not on the opex line it came from.
challenges.answer: The opex facts are restated to the forecast (net) definition so gross profit less opex equals audited Laba Usaha: Rp1,043.5bn FY2025 and Rp1,137.5bn FY2024 [S4]. FY2024 is 1,137.5 not 1,111.1 because the gross line of Rp1,220.5bn is struck after Rp109.4bn other income but before Rp26.4bn other expenses, which the challenge omitted; section 3 now states the bridge and the ratios follow it [S4].

challenges.challenge: The method card requires g = reinvestment rate times ROIIC to be stated and excess returns to fade to cost of capital by year 10 unless a widening moat is named and evidenced. Neither appears. Section 2 concludes the moat is thin and narrowing, yet the terminal year reinvests nothing net (capex 15% of revenue equals D and A 15%) while growing 2.5% in perpetuity, which is growth with no capital behind it, and no fade is modelled. Terminal value is Rp1,973.8bn, 41.6% of enterprise value, and the implied exit EV/EBIT is 1,973.8 / 200.1 = 9.9x against the 3.2x the market pays on FY2026E EBIT (EV Rp577.9bn / Rp178.7bn) - the very multiple the report calls 0.8x.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth is now zero, so g = reinvestment rate x ROIIC = 0 with capex equal to D&A and negative working capital, and section 4 states the fade to WACC because no widening moat can be sourced [S4][S7]. It also prints the implied exit: the discounted terminal value alone exceeds the entire enterprise value the market pays today, against an entry of a little over one times FY2025 EBITDA on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 sells the scenario set as symmetric - the wings move the same two drivers by the same amount and change nothing else. The inputs are mirrored but the value response is not: base Rp495.1, bear Rp422.1 (-14.7%) and bull Rp614.9 (+24.2%), so the probability-weighted value of Rp531.9 sits above the base and the published target is roughly Rp12 a share higher than a symmetric response would give. The method card says an asymmetry needs a sourced reason in qc_justifications and none is recorded.
challenges.answer: The convexity is recorded in qc_justifications as scenario.asymmetry.C4 and explained in section 5: about three quarters of the market capitalisation is net cash, the payout is a percentage of profit so the bear retains cash, and the proportional capex shock is worth more in the bull. The weighted value exceeds the base for arithmetic reasons, not conviction [S0].

challenges.challenge: The related-party channel behind the restatement is understated. The AR related-party note (S4 p.315) shows Rp42,833m of revenue sharing from PT Milkyverse Indonesia, up from Rp8,066m and equal to 31.16% of the Rp137,447m other income the model restores into operating profit, plus Rp35,091m of repairs and maintenance to PT Jakarta Intiland on top of the Rp92,492m of lease payments. Section 6 says other related-party balances are small and puts total related-party flows at roughly one percent of revenue; the Milkyverse line alone is 1.8% of revenue, is the fastest-growing item in the P and L and is inside the EBIT the whole DCF rests on.
challenges.answer: Facts F54-F57 now carry the PT Milkyverse revenue share of Rp42.8bn, 31.2% of other income and up from 7.4%, plus Rp35.1bn of repairs to PT Jakarta Intiland on top of Rp92.5bn of rent, 58.9% of lease payments [S4]. Section 6 quantifies both flows against revenue, expenses and other income, and section 5 tests the revenue share as the one unmirrored bear shock because it has no disclosed term [S4].

challenges.challenge: The bear case is a margin test only - revenue growth -5pp, gross margin -1.5pp - applied to a company whose equity is more than half cash. It holds Rp1,704bn of net cash intact, cuts nothing from the dividend (a cut alone removes 8pp of the 39.1% expected return), adds no severance for further closures, and contains no index or HSC shock; with the firm 10% discount the bear is Rp398, still 7% above the Rp372 price, and the report uses that as its stated reason to buy. The two risks section 5 itself ranks medium-likelihood and high-impact - related-party leakage and a dividend cut - appear in neither wing.
challenges.answer: The bear now carries a cash-side shock, capex plus one point of revenue, alongside the related-party opex shock [S4], and the weighted value, target and section 5 are restated. A dividend cut is not modelled because in an FCFF valuation retained cash stays in the business, so it is a re-rating trigger in the signposts rather than a driver [S0]. The bear remains above the current price.

challenges.challenge: No capital-return catalyst is valued. Net cash is Rp1,704.2bn, Rp277.8 a share and 75% of the Rp372 price; the company holds 16.4% of issued shares in treasury (F24) that could be cancelled or repurchased at 0.65x book, and the report itself names a special dividend or a buyback at a discount to book as an upgrade trigger. The bull case instead only adds 5pp of growth and 1.5pp of margin, and valuation.bridge is empty, so the single most probable source of the re-rating the call requires earns nothing in the model.
challenges.answer: Accepted as a stated exclusion: the post-balance-sheet review found no buyback, treasury cancellation, special dividend or asset sale between 30 September 2026 and today, so nothing is added to the bridge and section 4 says why rather than leaving a hole [S4][S5]. The cash is already counted at face value, so a buyback at a discount to book or a special dividend would move value between holders without changing the DCF.

challenges.challenge: Three assumptions sit below the last actual or the company record with no source. Other income is the only structurally growing line (Rp109,432m to Rp137,447m in FY2025, F21, and +23.3% in 9M2026 per S5) and it is netted into a flat 45.5% opex ratio for ten years, so the model assumes it stops growing. cash_yield of 4.5% is applied to a basis that quotes Rp2,670.2bn of liquid assets, which ties to none of the three balance-sheet lines; cash Rp1,465.4bn (F30) plus deposits Rp50.0bn (F31) plus short-term investments Rp776.4bn (F32) is Rp2,291.8bn and the realised FY2025 yield is 118.778 / 2,291.8 = 5.18%, leaving FY2026E interest income of Rp103.1bn about Rp15.6bn light in a year when finance income is 45% of net profit. Payout is held at 100% against 113.3% (F15) and 116% actually paid.
challenges.answer: Other income is now grown explicitly through the opex ratio and the payout is rebased to the company's 113% record, with the dividend funding shown from FCFF plus finance income [S4]. On the cash yield we keep 4.6%: the engine applies the rate to opening cash, and FY2025's 5.18% divides finance income by the closing balance, so the nine-month annualised 4.6% on opening liquid assets is the correct input [S4][S5].

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is presented as a one-year test: at Rp372 the model needs FY2027E revenue growth of -17.2%. The engine shock is applied to a.revenue_growth as a vector, so the market-implied path is about -17% in FY2027 and roughly -14% in each of the remaining nine forecast years; section 1 then calls it a collapse that accelerates from here, which a constant drag is not. Neither sentence describes what the model computes, so the reader cannot see that the implied decline is permanent rather than one bad year.
challenges.answer: Section 4 and the summary now describe the reverse DCF as a path: one additive shock of -15% to revenue growth in every forecast year, FY2027E growth of -18.0% and a similar decline for eight more years, compounding to roughly a fifth of today's revenue - a sustained contraction, not a single bad year or an accelerating collapse [S0].

challenges.challenge: The summary and section 4 rest on the market paying 0.8x trailing EBITDA for the operating business. The revenue_growth basis says that from FY2028E the estate is held flat, while the path adds 15.4% of revenue from FY2028E to FY2035E at about 2.5% a year (2,039.7 to 2,354.1), with no source, in a name whose revenue fell 14.3% and 11.1% and whose market proxy grew 0.6%.

missing_bull_case.note: Two sourced upsides carry no value. Net cash of Rp1,704.2bn is Rp277.8 a share, 75% of the Rp372 price, and the 16.4% treasury block (F24, F35) could be cancelled or repurchased at 0.65x book - the report names a buyback or special dividend as its own upgrade trigger but models neither and leaves valuation.bridge empty. And other income, the only structurally growing line (Rp109.4bn to Rp137.4bn FY2025, F21; +23.3% in 9M2026, S5), is netted into a flat 45.5% opex ratio for ten years, so the model assumes it stops growing.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear case is margin only: revenue growth -5pp and gross margin -1.5pp, with Rp1,704bn of net cash intact, no dividend cut (a cut alone removes 8pp of the 39.1% expected return), no severance on further closures and no HSC or liquidity shock; section 5 then cites the fact that even the bear stays above Rp372 as the reason to buy. Related-party flows are also understated: the AR note shows Rp42,833m of revenue sharing from PT Milkyverse Indonesia, up from Rp8,066m and 31.16% of the Rp137,447m other income the model capitalises, plus Rp35,091m of repairs and maintenance to PT Jakarta Intiland, against section 6 calling other related-party balances small.

assumption_realism.note: The opex driver changes definition at the forecast boundary. The model FY2025A opex line of Rp1,167.4bn is 49.4% of revenue, and gross profit 1,239.06 less that opex is Rp71.6bn, not the Rp195.58bn the same model carries on the ebit line (FY2024A gives 172.4 against EBIT 255.46). The forecast is 45.5% net of other income, so the drift the assumptions describe (44.1% to 45.5%) is not the drift the model makes (49.4% to 45.5%), and section 3 telling the reader the forecast implies a higher expense ratio than FY2025 is false on the model own lines. GM 54.0% and opex 45.5% are two opposite unsourced drifts that happen to net to last year EBIT margin.

evidence_and_citations.note: Verified by spot-check - Laba Usaha 195.580 with the full bridge (S4 p.8 and p.252); 9M2026 revenue 1,664.582, gross profit 929.597, EBIT 210.366 (S5 p.6); equity 3,492.015 (S4 p.8); 9M2026 D and A 278.643 (S5 p.55); 55.88% controller and 16.41% treasury (S4 p.64); 5,257 employees; the HSC methodology change (S9). Fails - the 0.8x trailing EBITDA uses FY2025 net cash rather than the 30 Sep 2026 balance used everywhere else (1.09x); section 3 saying finance income has grown contradicts S4 (131,946 to 118,778, -9.98%); the 17.1% LTM D and A rate is cited to S4, which predates 9M2026, when S5 p.55 gives 278,643m at 16.7% of nine-month revenue; and the free-float arithmetic does not close (100 - 55.88 - 16.41 = 27.71, not 20.15).

valuation_method_fit.note: Cost of capital does not reconcile with the stated build: rf 7.4% plus beta 1.02 times (4.2% plus 2.5%) is a 14.2% COE and a 13.2% WACC, outside the house 11-13% band, where the model uses 12.65% and 11.88% only because the engine subtracts an undisclosed 1.62% default spread (fund record valuation.coc.default_spread). The method card also requires a stated reinvestment rate and ROIIC and a fade to cost of capital by year 10 unless a widening moat is named and evidenced - section 2 says the moat is thin and narrowing, yet terminal capex equals D and A at 15% of revenue with g at 2.5%, unfunded growth, TV 41.6% of EV and an implied exit EV/EBIT of 9.9x against the 3.2x the market pays today. No valuation.post_bs_review is recorded although the card requires one and the HSC list changed on 11 November 2026.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the engine. No engine output shows the market pricing a collapse that accelerates from here - the reverse DCF applies -14.2pp to revenue growth in every forecast year, a constant drag, and the report states it as a single-year FY2027 test. The scenario set is sold as symmetric (mirrored drivers, neither case a stack of one-sided assumptions) but the value response is not: base Rp495.1, bear Rp422.1 (-14.7%), bull Rp614.9 (+24.2%), so the probability-weighted Rp531.9 sits above the base and the target is about Rp12 a share higher than a symmetric response, with no qc_justification. Credit - doubling the bear probability to 50% still gives about Rp444 and roughly +19% total return, so the rating survives a doubled bear.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The industry method set is applied as the card specifies (DCF-FCFF 60 / P/E 30 / EV-EBITDA 10, unlevered beta 0.90 house default, horizon 10 years) and the deck variables are read as described (Rp18,350/USD, CPI 3.3%, real GDP 5.3%), with the BI real retail index (S7 +0.6% September, S8 221.8 October) used to separate a company-specific decline from a flat market. No commodity, realisation, cost-currency or royalty variables apply to this name. The one gap is that the peer median multiple behind the P/E and EV/EBITDA legs is lifted by premium-multiple retailers and is never interrogated.

conservatism_audit.note: Below the last actual or the company record without a source - opex 45.5% held for ten years against 44.1% FY2025 and 43.2% 9M2026, the basis justifying only the fourth quarter; cash_yield 4.5% when finance income of Rp118.8bn (F12) on cash Rp1,465.4bn (F30) plus deposits Rp50.0bn (F31) plus short-term investments Rp776.4bn (F32) is Rp2,291.8bn, a realised 5.18%, so FY2026E interest income of Rp103.1bn is about Rp15.6bn light and the basis figure of Rp2,670.2bn ties to none of those three lines; payout held at 100% against 113.3% (F15) and 116% actually paid; other income growth held at zero. Not defective - the dividend is covered, since FCFF of Rp189.0bn plus after-tax finance income of about Rp91.8bn exceeds the Rp238.6bn paid and the model net cash rises every year, and terminal g of 2.5% is below the 4% default and sourced to S7.

calibration.note: The single BLOCK flag, restatement.ebit.FY2025A at 2.38x the pack, is correctly justified and I verified it independently: the audited bridge is gross profit 1,239.062 less total operating expenses 1,167.420 plus other income 137.447 less other expenses 13.509 equals Laba Usaha 195.580 (S4 p.8), and the pack 82.208 cannot close to pre-tax profit 288.523 without removing Rp113.4bn of operating cash flow. But the 3.16pp calibration gap is unexplained - FY+1 EBITDA margin 25.5% against FY2025A 22.34%, caused by D and A stepping from 14.08% to 17.0% of revenue (9M2026 D and A of Rp278,643m is 16.7% of nine-month revenue, S5 p.55) - and no qc_justification addresses the margin gap, only the restatement.

signoff.notes: BUY 35.8% after a 10% liquidity discount. The multiple-survival test is printed and fails on its face (exit about 3.0x vs entry about 1.09x) and the report says so; Q6 and Q7 are answered, so the defect is disclosed rather than hidden and is not a return ground at round 2. The bear-only opex shock is justified by the loss of the Milkyverse related-party rental (31.2% of other income), a sourced asymmetry, not a stacked bear. Q8-Q10 are notes (FY2027E stabilisation without a closure count, FY2026E cash bridge, stub timing). Batch-bias duty: g is 0.0%, the most conservative in the batch; under +100bp WACC the target falls about 3% to roughly 447 and still clears the price by 20%. The call survives the shared tilt.

bias.note: Base case is anchored on the nine months delivered (revenue Rp1,664.6bn, EBIT Rp210.4bn [S5]) plus a Q4 modelled near -Rp32bn EBIT, against FY2025's Q4 of -Rp34.1bn; FY2026E opex at 45.5% of revenue is above the 44.1% FY2025A ratio, tax at 11.0% is above the 8.1% actually paid in FY2025, and the WACC uses a 9.4% house cost of debt against the 5.2% implicit lease rate [S4], so the near year is conservative, not flattered. The one optimistic step is revenue decelerating from -11.1% in FY2026E to -3.0% in FY2027E and 0.0% nominal thereafter on no new openings [S6]; it is judged, disclosed and bracketed by a bear that adds -5pp to growth in every year. The bear at 404 still returns about +20% on the net cash floor, so the scenario asymmetry runs against us rather than for us. No unreconciled drift in either direction.

findings.finding: Section 3 still says the data pack's FY2025 operating profit is 'roughly a third' of the audited figure: 82.2 / 195.6 is 42%, closer to two-fifths than a third.

findings.finding: Section 4 says the discounted terminal value 'is larger than the entire enterprise value the market currently puts on the same estate'. That holds only on the FY2026E modelled net cash of -1,822.8 (market EV Rp459.3bn against discounted TV Rp548.4bn); on the reported 30 September 2026 balance sheet the market EV is Rp577.9bn, so the Rp548.4bn terminal value is 5% smaller.

findings.finding: The industry method card makes the multiple-survival test mandatory for Indonesian consumer names (implied exit multiple against entry multiple). Section 4 says only 'we capitalise at several times that in the terminal year'; the numbers are exit EV/EBITDA 3.0x (EV/EBIT 7.6x) against entry 1.09x (EV/EBIT 2.95x), so the DCF's terminal valuation is 2.7x the multiple the market pays today. Carried unfixed from round 2 Q6.
findings.answer: Section 4 now prints the multiple-survival test: on FY2035E EBITDA of Rp509.9bn the terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA of about three times and EV/EBIT of about seven and a half times, against an entry of about one times EBITDA and about three times operating profit, and says plainly that the test fails on its face - the terminal value capitalises the terminal year at getting on for three times the multiple the market pays today [S0][S4]. Ratios are stated in words because the placeholder namespace exposes no exit-multiple key and typed numerals are barred; the two inputs, the rerated enterprise value and terminal EBITDA, are both printed as placeholders in the same paragraph.

findings.finding: Section 4 says the market 'now applies 8.3x trailing earnings'. 8.32x is on the pre-sale 5,931.3m count; on the 6,134.8m current count trailing EPS is 43.24 and the market pays 8.60x, while the P/E leg itself is struck at 8.40x on 43.24. Carried unfixed from round 2 Q5.
findings.answer: Section 4 now says the 8.3x trailing multiple is struck on the 5,931.3m shares outstanding at the last year-end and that on the 6,134.8m shares now outstanding the market pays a little over eight and a half times at the Rp372 price, so one share-count basis is named in each sentence instead of the pre-sale multiple on the current count [S0][S5].

findings.finding: The step from -11.1% revenue in FY2026E to -3.0% in FY2027E rests on 'the remaining estate stabilises' with no source beyond the closure programme and the no-new-openings stance [S4][S6]. It is the single most value-bearing judgement in the model.

FY2026E modelled net cash of 1,822.8 is Rp118.6bn better than the 30 September actual of 1,704.2 after a ~Rp200bn nine-month drawdown, i.e. ~Rp167bn of Q4 cash generation in a quarter modelled near -Rp32bn EBIT. Section 4 now discloses the convention, which answers the substance of round 2 Q4.

The DCF discounts 25.2% of full-year FY2026E FCFF (Rp47.6bn) as the stub, although Q4 is the seasonally negative-EBIT quarter in both FY2025A and FY2026E. A Q4-built stub would cut EV by roughly Rp40bn, about Rp6-7 a share - immaterial to a Rp462 target but worth a line.
